```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_xgboost = requireNamespace("xgboost", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = has_xgboost)
```

Gradient boosting trains a sequence of models where each one corrects the errors of the ones before it.
Libraries such as xgboost do this with decision trees only. In rml any model can be the starting point of
another. A model's `gradient_transformers` are its **base models**: the model starts from their output and
learns to correct it, so it **boosts** them.

Throughout this vignette, "A is boosted by B" means A is a gradient transformer of B: A is the base model
and B learns the correction, `B = <class>(gradient_transformers = list(A))`.

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(rml)
set.seed(11)
n = 3000
X = data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rnorm(n), x3 = runif(n), x4 = rnorm(n))
logit = 1.2*X$x1 - 0.8*X$x2 + 2*(X$x3 > 0.6) + 1.5*X$x1*X$x4
y = as.numeric(runif(n) < 1/(1 + exp(-logit)))
train = sample(n, 2000)
gini = function(m) m$performance(X[-train, ], y[-train], metrics = 'gini')
```

## Regression: training on the residual

For a regressor, the gradient transformer's prediction g is subtracted from the target, so the model
learns `y - g`. At prediction the two are added back: `prediction = g + model output`. Here a linear
model is boosted by an xgboost regressor:

```{r regression}
y_reg = 3*X$x1 + 4*sin(3*X$x3) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)
lm_model = REG.STATS.LNR(name = 'lm')
lm_boosted_by_xgb = REG.XGBOOST(name = 'lm_xgb', nrounds = 100, max_depth = 3, eta = 0.1,
                                gradient_transformers = list(lm_model))
lm_boosted_by_xgb$fit(X[train, ], y_reg[train])
c(linear_model = lm_model$performance(X[-train, ], y_reg[-train], metrics = 'mae'),
  lm_boosted_by_xgb = lm_boosted_by_xgb$performance(X[-train, ], y_reg[-train], metrics = 'mae'))
```

Any regressor gets this behaviour automatically from the `REGRESSOR` base class.

## Binary classification: boosting in log-odds

For a classifier the correction is added on the log-odds (logit) scale:
`P(y = 1) = sigmoid(g + f(x))`, where g is the gradient transformer's logit and f is what the model
learns. The model must minimise the logistic loss of `g + f`, so this needs support from the algorithm.
These classifiers can boost a base model:

| Class | How g is used during training |
| --- | --- |
| `CLS.XGBOOST` | Passed to xgboost as the base margin of the training data, so trees fit the remaining log-odds. |
| `CLS.STATS.LR` | Passed to `glm` as an offset, so the regression fits the remaining log-odds. |
| `CLS.KERAS.DNN` | Fed as a second input and added to the network's linear output inside a custom logistic loss. |

A classifier used as a gradient transformer is always read on the logit scale. If it returns
probabilities they are converted to logits; if it already returns logits (`return = 'logit'`) they are
used as they are, so the conversion never happens twice. A gradient transformer must not use
`return = 'class'`.

A logistic regression boosted by xgboost, and an xgboost model boosted by a logistic regression:

```{r classification}
lr  = CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'lr')
xgb = CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'xgb', nrounds = 60, max_depth = 3, eta = 0.1)
lr_boosted_by_xgb = CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'lr_xgb', nrounds = 60, max_depth = 3, eta = 0.1,
                                gradient_transformers = list(lr))
xgb_boosted_by_lr = CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'xgb_lr', gradient_transformers = list(xgb))
lr_boosted_by_xgb$fit(X[train, ], y[train])
xgb_boosted_by_lr$fit(X[train, ], y[train])
c(logistic_regression = gini(lr), xgboost = gini(xgb),
  lr_boosted_by_xgb = gini(lr_boosted_by_xgb), xgb_boosted_by_lr = gini(xgb_boosted_by_lr))
```

Fitting `lr_boosted_by_xgb` also fitted `lr`, and fitting `xgb_boosted_by_lr` fitted `xgb`, because they
were not yet fitted. A gradient transformer that is already fitted is used as it is, so it can be a model
trained earlier on different data.

## Chains

A gradient transformer can have its own gradient transformers. "LR boosted by XGB, boosted by DNN" means
the logistic regression is the base model and a gradient transformer of the xgboost model, and the
xgboost model is a gradient transformer of the neural network:

```{r chain-dnn, eval = FALSE}
lr  = CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'lr')
xgb = CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'xgb', nrounds = 50, gradient_transformers = list(lr))
dnn = CLS.KERAS.DNN(name = 'dnn', num_layers = 2, epochs = 10, gradient_transformers = list(xgb))
dnn$fit(X, y)   # fits lr, then xgb on top of lr, then dnn on top of xgb
```

The same kind of chain with models available everywhere: a shallow xgboost boosted by a deeper xgboost,
boosted by a logistic regression:

```{r chain}
shallow = CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'shallow', nrounds = 30, max_depth = 2, eta = 0.1)
deep    = CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'deep', nrounds = 30, max_depth = 4, eta = 0.05, gradient_transformers = list(shallow))
top     = CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'top', gradient_transformers = list(deep))
top$fit(X[train, ], y[train])
c(shallow = gini(shallow), deep = gini(deep), top = gini(top))
```

## Several gradient transformers

When a model has more than one gradient transformer, their outputs are combined row by row with
`gradient_transformers_aggregator` (default `mean`) before the model learns the correction.

```{r multiple}
m = CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'multi', nrounds = 40, max_depth = 3,
  gradient_transformers = list(CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'g1', features.include = c('x1', 'x2')),
                               CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'g2', features.include = c('x3', 'x4'))))
m$fit(X[train, ], y[train])
gini(m)
```

## A fixed offset column

A gradient transformer can also be the name of a column of `X` holding a known offset (for example the
log-odds from an existing production model). Exclude it from the features if it should only act as an
offset.

```{r offset}
X$prior = qlogis(0.3)
m_off = CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'offset_model', nrounds = 30, gradient_transformers = list('prior'),
                    features.exclude = 'prior')
m_off$fit(X[train, ], y[train])
gini(m_off)
```

## Things to know

* Gradient transformers that are not fitted yet are trained on the same rows as the model they boost.
  Overfitting shows in out-of-sample performance (`performance()`, `performance.cv()`) and can be
  controlled inside xgboost and keras with validation data (`cv.set`, early stopping).
* Row sampling (`smp.method = 'upsample'` or `'downsample'`) keeps the gradient aligned with the sampled
  rows. SMOTE cannot be combined with gradient transformers, because synthetic rows have no
  gradient transformer output.
* Classifiers other than those in the table above stop with an error if given gradient transformers, because they cannot yet learn a
  correction on top of them. A class you write yourself can support them by using
  `attr(y, 'gradient')` in its `model.fit()` and overriding `supports_gradient_transformers()` to return
  `TRUE`.
